title: She Hid a Baby for Six Years While a Murderous Queen Ruled — And She Had No Idea What God Was Preserving
paragraphs: She Hid a Baby for Six Years While a Murderous Queen Ruled — And She Had No Idea What God Was Preserving

Athaliah thought she had erased the royal line. Somewhere inside the house of God, however, a child was breathing. For six silent years, heaven’s answer remained hidden—and the story of Jehosheba and Joash reminds us that what looks buried may actually be preserved.
Imagine hearing the footsteps.
Not ordinary footsteps.
The footsteps of people searching for children.

Somewhere inside the royal household of Judah, death had entered the corridors. A throne was suddenly empty. A dynasty was bleeding. A grandmother named Athaliah had apparently decided that the surest way to secure power was horrifyingly simple:
Destroy the royal heirs.
Then, in the middle of that nightmare, a woman reached for a baby.
Her name was Jehosheba.
And what she did next changed history.
The Hebrew of 2 Kings 11:2 describes the moment with startling force:
"וַתִּגְנֹב אֹתוֹ"
Vattignov oto.
Literally, she "stole him" or "snatched him away."
Not because the child belonged to someone else.
Because death was coming for him.

Joash was the son of the slain king Ahaziah. Athaliah, his grandmother, had seen that her son was dead and moved against the royal offspring. But Jehosheba—daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah—took little Joash from among the royal sons facing death and hid him with his nurse.
The biblical account says:
"וַיַּסְתִּרוּ אֹתוֹ מִפְּנֵי עֲתַלְיָהוּ, וְלֹא הוּמָת"
They hid him from Athaliah, and he was not put to death.
Read those final words again.
He was not put to death.
Athaliah had power.
She had soldiers.
She had the throne.
She had authority over the land.
But she did not have the final word.
And neither does whatever darkness is frightening you right now.
Because while Athaliah sat where everyone could see her, Joash lived where almost nobody could see him.
That may be one of the most hauntingly beautiful pictures in this entire story.
The counterfeit ruler was visible.
The preserved heir was hidden.
Evil looked established.
God's purpose looked absent.
Athaliah occupied the throne while the child connected to David's royal house was concealed.
For six years.
Not six days.
Not six weeks.
Six years.
Scripture says:
"וַיְהִי אִתָּהּ בֵּית יְהוָה, מִתְחַבֵּא שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים"
Vayehi ittah beit YHWH, mitchabbe sheish shanim.
He remained with her in the house of the LORD, hidden, for six years.
The Hebrew word מִתְחַבֵּא (mitchabbe) carries the sense of hiding or keeping oneself concealed.
Think about that.
A child whose existence threatened a throne was growing up quietly inside the house of God.
Outside, Athaliah ruled.
Inside, Joash grew.
Outside, wickedness appeared triumphant.
Inside, preservation continued.
Outside, people could have looked around and wondered what had happened to the royal house.
Inside, a little boy was waking up every morning.
Breathing.
Eating.
Growing.
Living.
Waiting without even understanding what he was waiting for.
And perhaps this is where the ancient story suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Because some of you know what it feels like to live through a season in which the wrong thing seems to be winning.
You prayed, but the situation got worse.
You obeyed, but the door stayed closed.
You tried to repair your marriage, but the silence remained.
You fought temptation, fell again, repented again, cried again, and wondered whether you would ever become the person you keep asking Christ to make you.
You buried someone you thought God would heal.
You watched somebody you love walk away from Jesus.
You lost something you thought was part of God's plan.
And perhaps the hardest part was not simply the pain.
It was the silence.
Because when God acts dramatically, faith feels easier.
But what happens when Athaliah is still on the throne in year two?
What happens in year four?
What happens when year six arrives and nothing visible seems to have changed?

This story does not give us permission to claim that every painful circumstance will end exactly as we want it to. Scripture never promises Christians a life without suffering. Jesus Himself told His disciples that they would have trouble in this world.
But this story does confront one dangerous conclusion:
Visible darkness does not prove divine absence.
Sometimes we assume that if God were working, we would already see it.
Joash challenges that assumption.
There was a living answer hidden inside the house of God while the nation could still see Athaliah reigning.
God's providence does not require publicity.
He can preserve something before He reveals it.
He can sustain something before anyone celebrates it.
He can work through a courageous woman whose name receives far less attention than the kings surrounding her.
And Jehosheba deserves to be remembered carefully.
She was not merely a convenient character inserted into Joash's story.
Second Chronicles gives us another crucial detail: Jehoshabeath—the variant form of her name—was the wife of Jehoiada the priest.
Think about the danger she accepted.
Athaliah was not some distant enemy.
This darkness existed inside Jehosheba's own family.
Jehosheba was Ahaziah's sister.
Joash was her nephew.
She stood at a terrible intersection of bloodline, danger, loyalty, and obedience.
She could have looked away.
She could have protected herself.
She could have whispered, "There is nothing I can do."
Instead, she picked up the child.
Sometimes courage does not look like standing before thousands.
Sometimes courage looks like quietly carrying one vulnerable person away from destruction.
Sometimes faithfulness is not a microphone.
It is a hiding place.
Sometimes nobody applauds the obedience that heaven uses.
No crowd watched Jehosheba rescue Joash.
No viral moment announced it.
No earthly audience knew how significant that act would become.
She simply did what had to be done.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that.
Your hidden obedience matters.
The prayer nobody hears matters.
The pornography you refuse to open tonight matters.
The apology you finally make matters.
The temptation you walk away from when nobody would have discovered it matters.
The child you keep teaching about Jesus even when you wonder whether they are listening matters.
The spouse you keep praying for matters.
The Bible you open while your emotions feel numb matters.
The integrity you maintain when compromise would be profitable matters.
The person you quietly encourage matters.
Not because these actions purchase God's love.
They do not.
We are not saved because we performed enough courageous acts.
We are saved by grace through faith, and our salvation rests ultimately in Christ and His finished work, not in our moral résumé.
But grace produces a changed life.
Real faith moves.
Jehosheba moved.
She took the child.
She hid him.
And for six years, the secret remained alive.
Then came the seventh year.
Jehoiada acted.
The guards were assembled. Covenants and oaths were made. The king's son was finally brought forward.
Imagine that moment.
Men who had lived under Athaliah suddenly saw something they may have thought was gone.
The king's son.
Alive.
Six years of concealment ended in revelation.
Joash was brought out, crowned, and publicly recognized. The people clapped and cried, "Long live the king!"
Athaliah heard the noise.
She came toward the temple.
And suddenly the woman who had occupied the throne discovered that the story had continued without her permission.
There stood the king.
The child she had failed to destroy.
Alive.

There is something profoundly Gospel-shaped in that movement—not because Joash is Jesus, and we should not force every detail into an allegory, but because the broader biblical story repeatedly teaches us that human rebellion cannot overthrow God's redemptive purposes.
And eventually Scripture takes us somewhere far greater than Joash.
To Jesus Christ.
Joash needed rescuing.
Jesus is the Rescuer.
Joash was an imperfect Davidic king who would later make grievous failures. Jesus is the righteous Son of David whose kingdom has no end.
Joash escaped death as a child.
Jesus willingly went into death for sinners.
Joash was hidden and later revealed.
Jesus was crucified publicly, buried, and on the third day rose victorious.
And this is where the story stops being merely fascinating history.
Because our deepest enemy is not an Athaliah somewhere outside us.
Our deepest crisis is sin within us.
We have all rebelled against God.
We have all tried, in countless ways, to occupy a throne that belongs to Him.
We want His blessings while resisting His authority.
We hide sins.
We protect idols.
We justify bitterness.
We rename lust.
We excuse pride.
We postpone repentance.
We become skilled at appearing spiritually alive while parts of our hearts are starving.
That is the scandal.
The scandal is not simply what Athaliah did.
The scandal is what sin has done to every one of us.
And then comes grace.
Jesus Christ does not save respectable people because they successfully repaired themselves.
He saves sinners.
The cross is where our excuses collapse and God's mercy shines.
The sinless Son of God bore sin.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The King wore thorns.
The Lord of glory was mocked.
The One through whom all things were made allowed nails to pierce His hands.
And He did not remain in the grave.
Jesus rose.
That changes everything.
Your past may explain wounds in you, but it does not possess the authority to forgive you.
Your shame can accuse you, but it cannot redeem you.
Your achievements can impress people, but they cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Christ can save.
And perhaps you have spent years hiding for an entirely different reason than Joash.
Joash was hidden for preservation.
You have been hiding because of shame.
There are things you hope nobody discovers.
Things you have deleted.
Things you have denied.
Things you remember at 2:00 in the morning.
Things you would never put beneath your Sunday photograph.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well.
You smile.
You work.
You serve.
You post Scripture.
You say, "God is good."
But privately you know there is a room in your soul you keep locked.
Jesus already knows what is inside it.
And still He calls you.
Not deeper into hiding.
Into repentance.
Into light.
Into grace.
Repentance is not paying God enough pain so He will tolerate you.
It is turning from sin and coming to the Savior who actually has authority to forgive.
You do not have to make your darkness prettier before bringing it to Christ.
Bring it into the light.
Confess.
Turn.
Trust Him.
Maybe your prayer tonight is not eloquent.
Maybe all you can say is:
"Jesus, forgive me."
Say it honestly.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we stop pretending.
Let somebody else reading know they are not the only believer fighting through a long night.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
Someone whose faith has become cold.
Someone quietly drowning in shame.
Someone who thinks God has abandoned them because evil seems to be winning.
Someone who needs to remember that six years of hiddenness did not mean God had surrendered the story.
There may come a night when Athaliah seems to be winning again, and you will need the reminder:
The throne you can see is not always the whole story.
The purpose is simple: daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this work, there is another way to stand with the mission.
It does not. Not because Christians must pay money to prove that they glorify God. Scripture does not teach that, and we will not pretend that it does.
We glorify God by belonging to Christ and living faithfully before Him.
But one way believers may freely choose to glorify God with what He has entrusted to them is by supporting Gospel-centered work that helps put biblical truth before more people.
Because somebody in your circle may be living through their sixth year.
Somebody may have mistaken God's silence for God's absence.
Somebody may think their sin is too filthy for Christ's blood.
Somebody may be one honest prayer away from finally admitting, "Jesus, I need You."
And perhaps God will use something as ordinary as your share to put His Word in front of them.
Jehosheba probably could not see everything her courageous act would mean when she reached for that endangered child.
She simply protected the life entrusted to her.
You may not know what God will do with one faithful act either.
Share.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because there are moments when faith becomes more real when we stop hiding behind polished words.
"Jesus forgive me."
"I'm still fighting."
"Pray for me."
"Christ is still healing me."
"No more hiding."
Whatever is true, say it.
Because the final beauty of Jehosheba's story is not merely that she successfully hid a baby.
It is that while evil was making noise in the palace, something precious was still alive in the house of God.
Athaliah had the throne for six years.
But she never owned the story.
And whatever chapter you are living through today, remember this:

The darkness may occupy the throne for a season, but it never gets to hold the pen over God's redemptive story—and at the center of our hope stands Jesus Christ, crucified for sinners, risen from the grave, and still rewriting lives that everyone else thought were finished.
